scope: ATT&CK Enterprise 20.1: Initial Access + Credential Access
provenance: Drafted by Claude in analyst language (mostly avoiding technique names), reviewed and approved by the project owner.

questions.question: Staff got emails with a link to a fake Microsoft login page. What is this and how do we detect it?
A Word document attached to an email ran macros when opened. What technique is this?
Someone called our help desk pretending to be IT and got a user to install remote-access software.
Attackers messaged employees on LinkedIn and sent them malware.
One common password was tried against hundreds of accounts to avoid lockouts.
Username/password pairs from another company's breach are being tried on our login page.
Attackers have password hashes and are recovering the plaintext offline with GPUs.
How do I detect someone reading the memory of the Windows process that holds logon credentials?
An attacker copied the Active Directory database file off a domain controller.
An attacker used replication permissions to pull password hashes from a domain controller.
Service tickets were requested for accounts with SPNs so they could be cracked offline.
Attackers forged Kerberos tickets with the krbtgt account's hash.
Users are flooded with MFA push prompts until someone taps approve.
Attackers stole browser session cookies to skip the login entirely.
A malicious app tricked users into granting OAuth consent, and its access token was stolen.
A compromised cloud VM queried 169.254.169.254 to get credentials.
Plaintext passwords were found in scripts and config files on a file share.
Malware pulled the passwords people had saved in Chrome.
The macOS keychain was dumped.
Attackers answered LLMNR/NBT-NS lookups to capture NTLM hashes.
A rogue access point used the same name as our corporate Wi-Fi.
Software on a workstation recorded every keystroke, including passwords.
Attackers got in through our internet-exposed VPN, which had no MFA.
An unpatched bug in our public web server was exploited to get inside.
Visitors to a legitimate but compromised website were infected through their browser.
Malicious code was slipped into an open-source package we depend on.
Attackers came in through our managed service provider's access to our network.
A device's default admin password was never changed, and attackers used it.
A USB drive found in the parking lot infected a computer when it was plugged in.
Attackers forged SAML tokens with a stolen signing certificate.
